cim: Artificial Intelligence Enables Accurate Cephalometric Analysis From Lateral Facial Photographs
cim_eredeti: Artificial Intelligence Enables Accurate Cephalometric Analysis From Lateral Facial Photographs
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial Intelligence Enables Accurate Cephalometric Analysis From Lateral Facial Photographs

A deep learning model utilizing a dual-task architecture—HRNetV2 coupled with an adaptive multilayer perceptron (MLP)—has successfully predicted lateral cephalometric measurements directly from lateral facial photographs, providing a feasible, radiation-free alternative to traditional cephalometric radiographs. Orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning have long relied on lateral cephalometric radiographs, introduced in 1931, to evaluate skeletal and dental malocclusions, monitor growth in adolescents, and assess pre- and post-treatment progress. However, manual landmark identification on these radiographs is time-consuming, requires significant expert skill, and is subject to intra-observer and inter-observer variability. The research team behind this new study aimed to mitigate these clinical limitations by developing a computational framework capable of automated landmark localization and cephalometric analysis using readily available facial photographs, thereby eliminating the need for ionizing radiation exposure associated with traditional cephalometric imaging.

To develop and evaluate the model, the researchers collected pretreatment records of 1,500 patients exhibiting various malocclusions, treated at the Faculty of Dentistry, Cairo University, between October 2020 and October 2024. This extensive dataset was divided into an independent test set of 150 patients, which remained concealed throughout the training and validation phases, while the remaining 1,350 records served as the development set. The researchers performed manual landmark identification for 19 skeletal, dental, and soft tissue landmarks using Dolphin imaging software to establish the ground truth. Corresponding lateral profile photographs, captured under standardized lighting and positioning, were processed to resize and rescale the images, followed by an image superimposition protocol that accurately transferred the cephalometric tracings onto the facial photographs. This rigorous verification ensured that the transferred coordinates served as a reliable basis for training the artificial intelligence system, which was then subjected to a series of preprocessing steps, including normalization and data augmentation, to enhance its robustness against variations in patient positioning or photographic technique.

The technical architecture employed a two-stage ensemble system designed to optimize precision in landmark prediction. The primary detector, HRNetV2, was configured to perform two simultaneous tasks: landmark coordinate regression, which focuses on local precision, and skeletal pattern classification based on the ANB angle, which provides essential global understanding. This dual-task approach enabled the model to use global skeletal morphology to inform the localization of specific, local landmarks. To further improve accuracy, the developers integrated an adaptive multilayer perceptron (MLP) as a tutor network. This secondary component was trained to identify the characteristic patterns of error generated by the HRNetV2 detector and subsequently output refined landmark coordinates. The training process utilized the Adam optimizer and was guided by a combined loss function that weighted the regression task twice as heavily as the classification task, with additional weighting applied to underrepresented skeletal class III cases to ensure balanced performance across all diagnostic categories.

In terms of performance, the ensemble-MLP model achieved a mean radial error of 2.317 ± 1.80 millimeters. The success detection rates, which track the percentage of landmarks falling within a defined distance threshold of the ground truth, were 53.8% at the 2-millimeter threshold and 84.5% at the 4-millimeter threshold. An analysis of the landmark-specific performance revealed that soft tissue landmarks, such as the nasal tip, subnasale, and upper and lower lips, demonstrated the lowest localization errors, with a mean radial error of 1.101 millimeters. This high performance in soft tissue markers is attributed to the distinct visual contours and stronger contrast inherent in the facial profile photographs. Conversely, posterior skeletal landmarks such as the Sella, Gonion, and PNS exhibited higher localization errors, a result consistent with previous research that highlights the complex anatomical definitions and greater inter-individual variability of these deeper, often virtual, landmarks.

The team also assessed the accuracy of automated cephalometric measurements derived from the predicted landmark coordinates by comparing them to ground truth measurements obtained from traditional cephalometric tracings. The mean absolute error for the ANB angle was calculated at 1.46 degrees, indicating high accuracy for this particular skeletal measurement. Bland-Altman analysis was employed to assess the agreement between the AI-derived measurements and the Dolphin-software-generated benchmarks. This analysis revealed minimal systematic bias across most evaluated parameters, with 95% confidence intervals for the mean bias including zero for nearly all cephalometric variables. These statistical findings confirm that the AI model produces results with no clinically relevant systematic differences when compared to the established gold-standard software, supporting the clinical potential of the photographic-based approach for routine orthodontic screening and longitudinal monitoring.

A critical component of the study was the assessment of model consistency across the three skeletal classes: class I, II, and III. Despite the imbalanced distribution of patient records in the initial sample—with class II being the most frequent and class III the least—the researchers successfully utilized class-weighted loss functions to ensure comparable accuracy across all categories. Statistical evaluation using the Kruskal-Wallis test showed no significant differences in mean radial error (p=0.147) or success detection rates at 2 millimeters (p=0.075) and 4 millimeters (p=0.055) between the skeletal groups. This consistent performance indicates that the model effectively compensated for data imbalance, demonstrating high robustness regardless of the skeletal malocclusion classification. The incorporation of the tutor MLP network was specifically found to provide a modest but consistent improvement in both landmark localization and angular measurement precision, confirming its role as an effective feature-refining mechanism within the larger ensemble architecture.

When comparing these findings with existing literature on cephalogram-based prediction, the model’s mean radial error of 2.317 millimeters falls well within the range of 1.4 to 3.4 millimeters reported in previous studies that relied on traditional radiographs. While the model showed slightly lower detection rates at the restrictive 2-millimeter threshold compared to some radiographic studies, it demonstrated highly comparable performance at the 4-millimeter threshold. The study emphasizes that while this AI-driven photographic approach is a significant technological advancement, it is intended to enhance rather than replace traditional radiographic assessment. The ability to predict these measurements without radiation exposure is particularly valuable for applications such as preliminary orthodontic screening, remote patient evaluation, and the frequent longitudinal tracking of treatment progress, where minimizing cumulative radiation dose is a clinical priority.

Despite these promising results, the researchers acknowledged several limitations that require further investigation. The current study was conducted using data from a single center, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to broader populations.
